title: Common Extension Categories
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Common Extension Categories.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to additional data types.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Common Extension Categories. Its primary job is to help you evaluate extensions, foreign-data access and internals while controlling trust, compatibility and operational scope. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing common extension categories teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: evaluate extensions, foreign-data access and internals while controlling trust, compatibility and operational scope. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

items.title: Additional data types
items.text: Relate this point to common extension categories: define the expected behavior, one edge case, and a query or check that would provide evidence.

items.title: Specialized indexes
items.text: Match the index method and operator class to real query predicates, then compare the plan and write/storage costs.

items.title: Text-search and similarity capabilities
items.text: Test representative queries, tokenization and ranking; optional extension features must be enabled and reviewed separately.

items.title: Diagnostics and development helpers
items.text: Capture the time, database, role and exact diagnostic; separate the original failure from symptoms before changing settings.

items.title: Evaluating compatibility and maintenance status
items.text: Prefer additive changes first, test against populated sample data, and preserve compatibility while old and new code overlap.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Common Extension Categories
content_blocks.code: SELECT extname, extversion FROM pg_extension ORDER BY extname;
content_blocks.expected_output: Lists extensions enabled in the current database; an empty result means none are installed there.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in the database being inspected. Availability on disk is a separate question from installation in this database.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Version note: PostgreSQL 18.6 is the primary reference. PostgreSQL 19 beta/development features are not assumed to be stable.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Common Extension Categories”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Additional data types”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Additional data types”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Common Extension Categories, with an explanation of “Additional data types”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Common Extension Categories fits into the broader goal to evaluate extensions, foreign-data access and internals while controlling trust, compatibility and operational scope.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Additional data types, Specialized indexes, Text-search and similarity capabilities.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
